title: Fix 'Permission denied' when > writes into a root-owned system file
summary: The > sign is handled by your own shell, so it writes with your rights. A system file such as /etc/hosts belongs to root, so the write is refused. Use sudo with tee to add the line with administrator rights.

prerequisites: An account that is allowed to use sudo; you will be asked for your password, and nothing appears while you type it

steps.explain: Check who owns the file. If the owner is root and the permissions give others no write access, your user cannot write to it, whatever the command. Replace <FILE> with the file that refuses the write.

placeholders.name: FILE
placeholders.description: The file that refuses the write

steps.expect: A line such as '-rw-r--r-- 1 root root ... /etc/hosts'. The owner is root, so only root can write to it.

steps.explain: Add a line to the file with administrator rights. tee -a writes the text at the end of the file and keeps the rest; it also prints the line on screen. The > sign cannot be used here because your shell opens the file before sudo runs. Replace <TEXT> with the line to add and <FILE> with the file.

placeholders.name: TEXT
placeholders.description: The line to add to the file

placeholders.name: FILE
placeholders.description: The file to add the line to, the same as in step 1

steps.expect: The line you added is printed on screen. No 'Permission denied' message appears.

alternatives.explain: Open the file in the nano text editor with administrator rights, add the line by hand, press Ctrl+O and Enter to save, then Ctrl+X to close. This is the safer choice when you want to see the whole file.
alternatives.expect: A text editor opens and shows the contents of the file.

alternatives.explain: Run the whole redirect inside a root shell. The text is inside single quotes, so the > is run by root.

placeholders.name: TEXT
placeholders.description: The line to add to the file

placeholders.name: FILE
placeholders.description: The file to add the line to

alternatives.expect: No output, and the prompt comes back. The line is now at the end of the file.

steps.explain: Check that the line is at the end of the file. Replace <FILE> with the same file as before.
steps.expect: The last lines of the file, and the line you added is the last one.

rollback.explain: Remove the line you added: open the file with administrator rights, delete that line, save and close.
rollback.expect: The file opens in the editor, and the added line is no longer there after you save.

warnings: Keep the -a in tee -a. Without -a, tee replaces the whole file with your text and the old contents are lost.
Changing /etc/hosts wrongly can break name resolution and internet access for some programs. Add only the line you need and remove it when you no longer need it.
Do not use sudo with > directly, as in 'sudo echo x > file': the > still runs as your user and fails the same way.
